II. The Question Presented Is Important and Warrants Review In This Case
Section 6853 Massively Intrudes on the Federal Courts
Section 6853, like Rule 8, Is Primarily a Rule of Procedure That Does Not Have to be Followed in Federal Court
Section 6853 Substantially Upsets the Balance Struck by the Federal Rules
REASONS FOR DENYING THE WRIT OF CERTIORARI
I. THE THIRD CIRCUIT’S UNPUBLISHED OPINION REFLECTS THE FACTBOUND APPLICATION OF SETTLED LAW
II. THERE IS NO CIRCUIT SPLIT WARRANTING THIS COURT’S REVIEW
A. The alleged circuit split is illusory because the outcome of the cases is the same when grouped according to the basis of federal-court jurisdiction
B. The circuit split claimed by Petitioner is also illusory because the specific terms of the various state statutes being applied differ in outcome-determinative ways.
III. THE THIRD CIRCUIT’S RULING IS CORRECT
IV. THIS CASE IS THE WRONG VEHICLE FOR REVIEW
I. The Circuit Conflict Is Square
A. The Conflict in this Case is Widely Recognized
B. Courts On the Long Side of the Split Have Expressly Rejected Any Distinction Between FTCA and Diversity Cases
C. The Delaware AOM Statute is Materially Similar to the Other AOM Statutes Examined in the Split
II. The Decision Below is Wrong
III. The Question Presented Is Important and This Case is An Ideal Vehicle
I. Delaware’s Law Requiring the Dismissal of a Complaint Unless it is Accompanied By an Affidavit Attesting to the Merit of the Claims Cannot be Applied in Federal Court
A. Under Shady Grove, if a Federal Rule and State Law Answer the Same Question, the Federal Rule Controls
B. Federal Rules 8 and 9 Answer the Same Question as Delaware’s Affidavit-of-Merit Law
C. Other Federal Rules Answer the Same Question as Delaware’s Affidavit-of-Merit Law
D. The Federal Rules Are Valid and Do Not Violate the Rules Enabling Act
E. The Third Circuit’s Conflict Analysis and Erie Analysis Were Both Wrong
II. The Court Should Stick To Its Plain-Meaning Approach to Procedural Conflicts
I. AFFIDAVIT OF MERIT REQUIREMENTS VARY FROM STATE TO STATE AND WOULD PRODUCE NEW BURDENS ON DISTRICT COURTS
A. Incorporation of an Affidavit of Merit Requirement Undercuts the Way in Which the Federal Rules Operate
B. States Vary in What Is Required of an Affidavit or Certificate of Merit, But the Contents Often Become Disputes Between the Parties
1. Satellite litigation occurs over the expert’s qualifications
2. Satellite litigation occurs over the substance of the certificate
3. Incorporation of state affidavit of merit requirements would extend beyond medical malpractice cases
II. AFFIDAVIT REQUIREMENTS UNNECESSARILY INCREASE THE COSTS OF MEDICAL-MALPRACTICE LITIGATION
III. AFFIDAVIT REQUIREMENTS HAVE UNDESIRABLE SPILLOVER EFFECTS IN LITIGATING THE MERITS OF A CLAIM
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
I. State laws requiring dismissal of complaints because they are unaccompanied by expert affidavits should not apply in federal court
A. Delaware’s requirement that plaintiffs file an expert affidavit of merit with their complaint conflicts with the Federal Rules of
B. H olding that state affidavit-of-merit requirements apply in federal court would produce satellite litigation and cause confusion in other areas
C. Affidavit-of-merit requirements prevent some parties with meritorious claims from seeking justice
D. Allowing Petitioner’s case to proceed would neither cause forum shopping nor harm medical care
THE DECISION BELOW SHOULD BE REVERSED BECAUSE SECTION
CONFLICTS WITH MANY OF THE FEDERAL RULES OF CIVIL PROCEDURE
Section 6853 Massively Intrudes on the Federal Courts
Section 6853, like Rule 8, Is Primarily a Rule of Procedure That Does Not Have to be Followed in Federal Court
Section 6853 Substantially Upsets the Balance Struck by the Federal Rules
I. UNTANGLING THE INCREASINGLY COMPLEX ERIE ANALYSIS WOULD AID LOWER COURTS AND PROMOTE GREATER UNIFORMITY
II. SHADY GROVE WAS A SMALL STEP TOWARDS A RETURN TO BASICS
III. CASES INVOLVING AFFIDAVIT-OF- MERIT STATUTES HIGHLIGHT THE COMPLEXITY OF THE CURRENT ERIE ANALYSIS
IV. THIS COURT SH OULD DECLARE A RULE THAT CLARIFIES AND SIMPLI- FIES THE ERIE ANALYSIS
A. Delaware enacted various reforms to regulate medical negligence claims, including an affidavit-of-merit requirement to limit meritless pro se litigation
B. Petitioner filed this litigation in federal court without an affidavit of merit and, despite receiving nearly five months to obtain one, failed to do so
C. The Third Circuit affirmed dismissal due to Petitioner’s failure to comply with Delaware law
I. Petitioner’s characterization of Hanna’s “direct collision” test, and Shady Grove’s application of it, is inaccurate
A. The Federal Rules directly collide with a state-law provision only if they leave no room for the provision to operate
B. The Federal Rules do not directly collide with a state statute merely because it “refer[s] to procedures in state courts.”
II. Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement must be enforced in federal court
A. There is no direct collision under Hanna because Rule 11(a) expressly instructs federal courts to apply state statutes requiring a complaint to be “accompanied by an affidavit.”
B. To manufacture a direct collision under Hanna, Petitioner distorts seven different Federal Rules to create conflicts where none exist
C. Erie requires Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement to be enforced in federal court
III. In the alternative, adopting Petitioner’s expansive interpretation of the Federal Rules would violate the Rules Enabling Act
I. The District Court’s Application of Delaware’s Affidavit-of-Merit Requirement Did Not Conflict with the Federal Rules
A. Rule 11 Makes Clear that the Federal Rules Neither Impose Nor Preempt Any Requirement that a Plaintiff File an Affidavit Accompanying a Complaint
B. The Federal Rules Do Not Answer Whether an Affidavit Must Be Submitted Early in a Case
1. Petitioner Mischaracterizes the Governing Legal Framework and the Delaware Law
2. Delaware’s Affidavit-of-Merit Requirement Does Not Conflict with Any Federal Rule
C. At Minimum, Federal Courts Properly Grant Judgment to a Defendant When a Plaintiff Is Unable to Secure an Affidavit of Merit
II. Petitioner’s Proposed Application of the Rules Would Violate the Rules Enabling Act
III. The Evidentiary Showing Demanded by Delaware Law Is Substantive Under Erie
I. Proper Application of this Court’s Precedent Compels Affirmance, Giving Effect to Federalism Principles
II. Contextualizing Delaware’s Affidavit of Merit Requirement Against the Background of Medical Liability Reform
A. The challenges to healthcare and the medical community that affidavit of merit statutes address
B. Responding to the challenges: medical liability reform
C. Medical malpractice affidavit of merit laws are an integral part of state substantive policy governing healthcare access, affordability, and quality
III. Medical malpractice claims in federal court
IV. Consistent with the Erie doctrine, applying state affidavit of merit statutes in federal court ensures uniformity and gives effect to federalism principles
I. THE FEDERAL RULES REQUIRE ENFORCEMENT OF THE DELAWARE AOM STATUTE IN FEDERAL COURT, AND THE STATUTE PROMOTES THE OBJECTIVES OF THOSE RULES
II. ERIE REQUIRES FEDERAL COURTS TO APPLY DELAWARE’S AOM REQUIREMENT
I. The Rules Enabling Act authorizes procedural rules that do not abridge, enlarge, or modify substantive rights
A. The Rules Enabling Act establishes a twostep process for determining a Rule’s validity
B. This Court should clarify what constitutes a “substantive right” for purposes of § 2072(b)
II. Applying the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure to displace Delaware’s affidavit requirement would abridge or modify litigants’ substantive rights under state law
I. Meritless Medical Malpractice Claims Place Substantial Burdens On Providers, Patients, And Healthcare Systems As A Whole
A. Providers A nd Patients Suffer From The Proliferation Of Meritless Medical Malpractice Claims
B. Medical Malpractice Insurance Costs Burden The Healthcare System As A Whole
II. Affidavit Of Merit Requirements Are An Important Tool For Reducing Meritless Medical Malpractice Suits
III. This Court Should Reject Plaintiffs’ Attempt To Circumvent States’ Efforts To Safeguard Their Healthcare Systems
I. State Legislatures Enacted Affidavit of Merit Statutes to Prevent Meritless Lawsuits That Threaten the Availability of Quality, Affordable Healthcare
A. The Rise of “Nuclear” Verdicts Awarding Excessive Noneconomic Damages for Pain and Suffering Incentivized Meritless Lawsuits and Created an Insurance Crisis
B. State Legislatures Enacted Statutory Reforms to Address This Crisis and Protect Access to Quality, Affordable Healthcare
C. Meritless Claims Remain a Problem These Statutes Prevent
D. Meritless Medical Malpractice Claims Are Harmful to the Provision of Quality, Affordable Healthcare.
II. This Court Should Affirm That Shady Grove Represents a Straightforward Application of Hanna, Walker, and Burlington
III. State Affidavit of Merit Statutes Do Not— And Cannot—Directly Collide with the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Because They Provide Substantive Law
A. The State Legislative Policy Decisions Bound Up in Certificate of Merit Statutes Apply Equally in Federal Court

3. Courts refer to preliminary injunctions as prohibitory
or mandatory. Prohibitory injunctions maintain the status quo
pending resolution of the case; mandatory injunctions alter
it." N. Am. Soccer League, LLC, 883 F.3d at 36. "Because
mandatory injunctions disrupt the status quo," they are subject
to "a heightened legal standard by showing a clear or substantial
likelihood of success on the merits." ld. at 37 (internal quotation
marks omitted). In deciding whether a preliminary injunction is
mandatory or prohibitory, the Second Circuit has defined "status
quo" as "the last actual, peaceable uncontested status which
preceded the pending controversy." ld. (internal quotation marks
omitted). Because Plaintiff seeks to restore the status quo prior
to Defendant's alleged infringement, the heightened standard for
mandatory injunctions does not apply. See Two Hands IP LLC v.
Two Hands Am., Inc., No. 21 Civ. 3855, 2021 U.S. Dist. LEXIS
186969, 2021 WL 4437975, at *2 n.2 (S.D.N.Y. sept. 28, 2021)
he plaintiff seeks to halt the alleged infringement of its marks.
Such an injunction is generally considered to be prohibitory,
rather than mandatory." (citing Louis Vuitton Malletier v.
Dooney & Bourke, Inc., 454 F.3d 108, 114 (2d Cir. 2006))). Even
if the heightened standard applies here, it is satisfied because
Plaintiff has shown, not only a likelihood of success on the merits
as discussed in the text, but also a clear or substantial likelihood
of success on the merits.
